segmenti.tekst: Nahnu naqussu 'alayka ahsanal-qasasi bima awhayna ilayka hadhal-Qur'ana wa in kunta min qablihi laminal-ghafilin.

…upon his family, upon his companions, and upon all those who follow the path, the path of the Qur'an, the path of the Sunnah of Muhammad. In yesterday's lecture after the dawn prayer we spoke about the introduction to the surah, about Surah Yusuf.

We mentioned why Surah Yusuf got the name Yusuf, that is, why it was named after Yusuf, alayhis-salatu was-salam (peace be upon him), one of the best prophets, of the prophets of Allah mentioned in the Qur'an.
We also said that Yusuf is a man, or a prophet, of the most noble lineage: he is the son of a prophet, the son of a prophet, the son of a prophet.

That is, his father was a prophet, his grandfather was a prophet and his great-grandfather was a prophet. Yusuf, alayhis-salam, who in his childhood lived with his father Yaqub near present-day Al-Khalil, or, let's say, the city of Hebron.
Yusuf, alayhis-salam, who had eleven more brothers. His mother was called Rahil (Rachel), as some sources state.
And from this mother he had one full brother, Benjamin. That is as far as those who lived, that is, the relatives who lived with Yusuf, alayhis-salatu was-salam, are concerned.

It is interesting that Yaqub, his father, loved Yusuf, alayhis-salam, very much and singled him out in this respect from the other children. When Yusuf, alayhis-salam, turned 12, he saw, dear brothers, a dream.
A dream that would be, or that was, the introduction to everything that would happen to him later. A dream that would be the introduction to everything that would happen to him later.
And with this dream Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, gave glad tidings to Yusuf, alayhis-salatu was-salam. Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, says:
"Idh qala Yusufu li abihi ya abati." And say, O Muhammad, say to your companions: when Yusuf, alayhis-salam, said to his father: "Ya abati" – O my dear father.

What can we notice first in this verse? We can notice the upbringing of Yusuf, alayhis-salam, his fine upbringing. Yusuf, alayhis-salam, comes to his father – and here, dear brothers, the role of the parent is reflected.
Yusuf, alayhis-salam, did not go to his best friend, Yusuf, alayhis-salam, did not go to a neighbour and so on; rather, whom did he choose to tell the dream to? His father.
Why? Because the father is the main pillar and the best adviser. The father is the best adviser to his child. That is why, dear brothers, we must by no means [unclear] our fathers.
Also, what this verse points out to us is that we should not call our fathers by their names, but rather address them affectionately: "O my dear father."

And you also have examples where Ibrahim, alayhis-salam, addresses his father affectionately when he wants to tell him something: "My father, my dear father." That is how we too should be towards our parents, which is what this verse also points to.
Also, what this verse points to is that between Yusuf, alayhis-salam, and Yaqub there were no secrets, there were no closed files; rather, they were open with one another.
Rather, they were open with one another. That is how we too should be towards our children. When a child comes to tell us something, we should not turn him away.
Imagine, now your child or my child comes to tell us about some dream. Most of us will probably say: "Come on, for goodness' sake, go away for a bit, rest, play, take a nap."

Instead, the child should be given space to say what he wants, to express himself. Why? So that he gains a sense of security, so that he gains a sense of security. And it is up to the father, or up to the parent – up to the parent, especially the father. We see here how Yusuf, alayhis-salam, went to his father, to his father to seek, to seek advice.
And he says: "O my dear father, I saw in a dream 11 stars, the sun and the moon prostrating to me."
And his father interpreted this dream for him, saying that these 11 stars – those, he says, are your brothers; this sun – that is your mother;

and this moon, he says, that is your father, or me. And this is the introduction to everything that will happen to Yusuf, to the authority and power that Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, will give him in this world.
Someone may ask how it is that they would prostrate to him. Well, we see it mentioned in the Qur'anic verses as well, it says: "And when We said to the angels: prostrate to Adam."
In the earlier sacred laws there existed, dear brothers, that practice, or "tahiyyatus-sujud" – the prostration of greeting.

That is not a prostration of worship, as when we fall down in prostration to Allah, but a prostration of greeting. With the coming of the Sharia this ruling was abrogated, or abolished. It is mentioned there that when Mu'adh ibn Jabal came from Yemen and wanted to make a prostration of greeting to the Prophet, the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam (peace be upon him), forbade him to do so and said: "That is not part of my Sharia," and it was abolished.

That prostration, that prostration of greeting, was made to someone who held a high position, or to elderly people, or to those who came back from a journey, and that is how the prostration of greeting was performed.
As we said, it was abolished by the Sharia of Muhammad, of Muhammad. As we also said, this dream of Yusuf already leads into another sphere and into another life.

So we will, in sha Allah, continue tomorrow. Every day we will, in sha Allah, set aside some 6–7 minutes like this for this lecture. It will not be long, and I hope, in sha Allah, that it will be, in sha Allah, [unclear]. I ask Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, to reward you with every good. I ask Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, to reward you for your patience. I ask Him, the Exalted, to forgive us our sins. Amin, ya Rabbal-'alamin.
